summary: Chad lies inland in north-central Africa, with the Sahara Desert in the north and the Sahel and savanna in the south; the country's name comes from Lake Chad.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam arrived along the trans-Saharan trade routes, and in the 11th century the king of the Kanem Empire around Lake Chad converted to Islam, making it the religion of the ruling class. The Kanem–Bornu, Baguirmi and Wadai sultanates then successively made Islam their state religion and spread the faith across the Sahel through war and trade. Muslims are therefore concentrated in the north and center and are mainly Arab-descended and Sahelian peoples.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In the early 20th century, during French colonial rule, evangelical missionaries from the United States and Europe entered the south, preaching among peoples such as the Sara and running schools and clinics. The southern peoples had often been raided for slaves by the northern sultanates and so were less inclined to accept Islam, and Protestantism developed rapidly in the south. The division between northern Muslims and southern Christians also became part of the background of the Chadian civil wars since the 1960s.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Around 1929 French missionaries established mission stations in the south for Catholicism, then set up dioceses and ran schools. The colonial government promoted cotton growing and Western education in the south, and southerners educated by the church became the main elite of the government in the early independence period, such as the first president, Tombalbaye. Catholics are concentrated mainly in southern cities such as Moundou and Sarh.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Many people in the south still keep ancestor veneration and traditional rituals, but most are registered as Christians or Muslims, and very few clearly state that they have no religion. In Chadian society, where religion and ethnic identity are closely bound together, belonging to no religion is often seen as odd, so the share of non-religious people is extremely low and consists mainly of a few intellectuals in the capital, N'Djamena.

religion.background: Northern and central Chad has been influenced by Islam since the Kanem Empire of the 11th century, and sultanates such as Kanem–Bornu, Baguirmi and Wadai long held Islam as the state religion and raided the south for slaves. The southern peoples kept their traditional beliefs and accepted Catholicism and Protestantism on a large scale only during French colonial rule in the 20th century. The religious, ethnic and economic differences between northern Muslims and southern Christians deeply shaped the political antagonism and civil wars after independence in 1960.

language.official: French and Arabic are the official languages.

ranking.name: Chadian Arabic
ranking.description: Chadian Arabic derives from Arab nomadic tribes who moved west from the Nile Valley after the 14th century, intermarried with local peoples and brought their language. Because it is widely used in markets, trade and along herding routes, it gradually became the lingua franca among the various peoples, especially in the capital, N'Djamena. The 1996 constitution made Arabic an official language alongside French, but what is used in daily life is the Chadian dialect rather than Standard Arabic.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French is the administrative language introduced when France colonized Chad after defeating the warlord Rabih in 1900, and in 1910 Chad was incorporated into French Equatorial Africa. After independence in 1960 French remained the main language of government, courts and schools, but only educated people can use it fluently, so the actual share is not high and it is mostly a second language.

language.history: Chad has more than a hundred languages, belonging to the three great families of Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Niger–Congo, and Sara in the south is one of the largest indigenous language groups. From the Middle Ages the westward movement of Arab nomads made Chadian Arabic the trade lingua franca of the Sahel. After French colonization in 1900 French became the language of administration and education. After independence the southern elites governed in French, while the north demanded a higher status for Arabic, and the 1996 constitution finally made the two official languages together.

ranking.name: Boule
ranking.description: Millet, sorghum or maize flour is cooked with water into a thick dough, served in a ball shape, and a small lump is pinched off by hand and dipped in okra sauce or meat stew.
ranking.history: Millet and sorghum have been the most drought-resistant food crops of the Sahel for thousands of years, and cooking grain into a thick paste is a way of eating shared by the peoples of Chad, called "aïsh" in Arabic. French-speaking residents in the colonial period called it "boule" (ball) because of its round shape, and the name has been used ever since. It is almost the staple that Chadians eat every day, and it is an important family custom for the whole family to sit around one large dish and eat together.

ranking.name: Kisra
ranking.description: Fermented sorghum batter is spread extremely thin on a hot iron griddle to make a large flatbread, slightly sour and soft, torn into small pieces and dipped into stews or sauces.
ranking.history: Kisra is a traditional staple of Sudan, and the Wadai region of eastern Chad has long had contact with Darfur in Sudan, through which trade, nomadic migration and intermarriage brought this flatbread into eastern Chad. After the Darfur conflict broke out in 2003, large numbers of Sudanese refugees poured into refugee camps in eastern Chad, which further spread kisra there. It is popular mainly in the east and in Arab-descended families, and making it requires skilled technique to spread it thin and even.
ranking.imageCredit: Mohamed Elfatih Hamadien・CC BY-SA 4.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Okra stew (sauce gombo)
ranking.description: Fresh or sun-dried and ground okra simmered with meat, dried fish and tomato, with a thick, slippery broth, the main sauce eaten with boule.
ranking.history: Okra is native to Africa and was grown early in the Sahel and West Africa, where it is one of the most important vegetables. Chadians often dry and grind okra to keep it, so that a thick sauce can be cooked even in the dry season. The word "gombo" derives from a Bantu language and later spread to the Americas with the slave trade, becoming the name of the "gumbo" soup of Louisiana in the United States, which shows the influence of this dish on African food history.

ranking.name: Daraba
ranking.description: Okra, eggplant, sweet potato, tomato and spinach cut into pieces and stewed with peanut butter, rich and slightly sweet.
ranking.history: Daraba is a traditional stew of southern Chad, where rainfall is higher and suitable for growing a variety of vegetables. The peanut is native to South America and became common in Africa after the Portuguese brought it, and in the French colonial period southern Chad was also required to grow cash crops such as cotton and peanuts in large quantities. Peanut butter adds fat and protein to this vegetable stew, so it is an important home dish in the southern countryside.

ranking.name: Karkanji (hibiscus drink)
ranking.description: Dried hibiscus calyces are steeped in water to draw out a deep red liquid, flavored with sugar, ginger, clove or mint, and served ice cold, sweet-sour, refreshing and very thirst-quenching.
ranking.history: Hibiscus is native to Africa and grows well in the hot, dry climate of the Sahel, where it is an important crop. Chadians call this drink "karkanji," which belongs to the same tradition as Sudan's "karkade" and West Africa's "bissap." Because Muslims do not drink alcohol, hibiscus drink is the most common beverage at weddings, religious holidays and the breaking of the fast in Ramadan, and it is also an inexpensive cold drink sold by street vendors.
